content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers adaptive gradient methods for optimization, which are commonly used to train deep neural networks across a variety of domains. In some domains, adaptive methods suffer degraded generalization relative to methods like SGD with momentum (this problem has been addressed by many papers, but it seems that is still has not yet been solved fully!). Within this work, the authors proposed a modification to the adaptive gradient method Adam that solves this problem. In particular, the authors replace gradient in the second moment estimate term of Adam with a “momentumized” version of the gradient, which provides more accurate directional information. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the algorithm and show that the approach will generalize better than vanilla Adam (in expectation). Furthermore, the algorithm is shown to outperform a wide range of different baselines (including SGDM) across a large number of experimental domains, including image classification, language modeling/translation, and generative modeling.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* The method is quite simple and introduces no additional overhead. Additionally, it seems to provide added robustness to the setting of hyperparameters. 
* The motivation is clear and understandable — using the momentum version of the second moment estimate is more smooth and better reflects accurate directional information. 
* Provide convergence guarantees for the modified optimizer, as well as show the generalization of Adam^3 is better than Adam in expectation. These convergence rates also improve upon prior work to the best of my knowledge and remove some unrealistic constraints, which is impressive. 
* Properly addresses prior work that studies closing the generalization gap between SGDM and adaptive methods — this is a common topic that has been previously explored. Very interesting to learn that most of these approaches still do not fully solve the problem of poor generalization for adaptive methods.
* Provide experiments across various domains, including large-scale datasets. The experimental results are comprehensive and well-done. A large number of different baseline optimizers are used for comparison

Weakness:
* Still outperformed by SGDM in a few cases, but I think this is minor. The results are overall pretty impressive empirically — Adam^3 seems to match (and often improve) SGDM performance most of the time. 
* In general, I think the clarity of the writing could be improved. My biggest concern is Section 2, which I think could be easily re-written in a much clearer manner. 
* The organization of the paper could be improved, the current structure (in my opinion) is a bit random and hard to follow. E.g., two different theoretical results are provided both within Section 3. The clarity of the work could be drastically improved by providing a more clear outline of the work in the introduction, then structuring the paper into distinct components based on this outline. 

Small Stuff:
* Is it possible you should replace saying you “momentumize” the gradient in the abstract etc. by just saying you use EMA? To me, it might not be clear what you mean by momentum in this case, whereas saying that you use EMA is precise. This is just a small thought to include clarity in the abstract and introduction portions of the writing.
* “the EMA of the gradient is a more accurate estimation of the appropriate direction to descent”: To me, this makes intuitive sense, but is there a citation or some proof of this being correct? It seems like maybe a little more elaboration could be provided to support this claim. 
* In section 2, it would be good to explicitly define Adam and Adam^3, then highlight the difference between the two. I know that a description of various optimizers is provided, but I found this a bit difficult to follow. It is mostly a bunch of text explaining different adaptive methods, and I think providing and explicit definition/comparison between Adam and Adam^3 would make this way clearer (it seems like you do this somewhat in Eq. 2, maybe you can move this earlier or add it into the previous section as well?)
* The 1D example provides some nice intuition for your optimizer. This is well done.
* Misspelling at beginning of Sec. 3.2 “equalts”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In general, my main concern with the paper is clarity. I think the writing and structure of the paper could be improved a lot, which would make the paper more clear and easy to understand. Novelty and reproducibility are good.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe that the paper should be accepted. A basic summary of my main reasons for acceptance is as follows:
* This work address a clear and known problem. Various prior works have attempted to solve this problem, but it seems that they have been less successful than this work. 
* The proposed approach is very simple and works incredibly well in experiments across a comprehensive list of domains.
* The authors provide extensive theory to support this method, which even removes existing constraints that are used within prior work. The theory (to the best of my knowledge) provides a useful contribution relative to prior work.

Currently, I believe the clarity of writing in the work is somewhat poor. I do not think this should be a reason for rejection whatsoever. The paper is very good already, but I think putting time into re-structuring/writing will make it significantly better. I strongly advise the authors to spend time improving the writing within this work. I believe the ideas within this paper have great potential and should be explained as clearly as possible.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Adaptive gradient methods, e.g., ADAM, are observed to suffer from compromised generalization capacity compared with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and tend to be trapped in local minima at an early stage during the training process. The authors claim that they discover that the issue can be resolved by substituting the gradient in the second raw moment estimate term with its momentumized version in ADAM. The authors state that the gradient with momentum contains more accurate directional information, and therefore its second moment estimation is a more preferable option for learning rate scaling than that of the raw gradient. Thereby the authors propose ADAM^3 as a new optimizer reaching the goal of training quickly while generalizing much better.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The paper is sort of easy to follow.


2. The authors tested the performance of Adam^3 on various different tasks.


Weakness:


1. The authors state that "Despite their fast speed in the early training phase, adaptive gradient methods, especially Adam, are found by studies (Wilson et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2020) to be more likely to exhibit poorer generalization ability than SGD (M). This is discouraging because the ultimate goal of training in many machine learning tasks is to exhibit favorable performance during the testing phase." --- This statement seems incorrect to me. As far as I am aware, training deep neural networks using Adam is often much better than using SGD (M), including training Recurrent neural networks, transformers for NLP tasks, vision transformers for vision tasks, and generative adversarial networks.


2. The authors state that "Since the EMA of the gradient is a more accurate estimation of the appropriate direction to descent, we consider putting it in the second moment estimation term as well."--- What is the intuition of EMA of the gradient is a more accurate estimation? In Adam, the second moment is already a moving average of the square of the gradient. Replacing g_t^2 with m_t^2 in estimating the second moment v_t seems simular to using a smaller beta_2.


3. epsilon has already been added into Adam for numerical stability guarantee. If putting epsilon inside the square root affects the performance, I want the authors to do an ablation study. Also, the authors should contrast AdaM^3 with Adam using different values of epsilon. 


4. The explanation in section 3.1 is unconvincing. 1) In area A, when |g_t| increases, both v_t and m_t increase, the the update \alpha*\hat{m}_t/\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} does not really decays significantly. If both step size and \hat{m}_t are very large, the stability of the optimizer will be a concern. Similarly, I do not agree with the other points in section 3.1. The argument on the discussion of the benefit of changing the location of \epsilon merely shows that \epsilon matters, and by using a larger \epsilon for Adam, Adam becomes similar to AdaM^3.


5. Assumption 3 is not true; clearly, the gradient direction is very different from the direction of m_t. 


6. The discussion in section 3.2 does not imply AdaM^3 generalizes better than Adam. First, there are a lot of arguments about flat minima; whether this implies better generalization is not something for sure. Second, some assumptions in section 3.2 do not hold. 3. The authors should at least design a simple toy example that contains one flat and one non-flat minimum to show that 1) flat minima generalize better and 2) AdaM^3 converges to the flat one.


7. As far as I am aware, the theory in section 4 does not really better than the existing theory of Adam-style algorithms.


8. Tuning \beta_2 and \epsilon for Adam will make Adam have the same behavior as AdaM^3. I want the author to comment on this.


9. For the experiment in section 5.1: 1) How about testing the quadratic functions whose level sets are ellipses of different ratios between x- and y-axis? 2) How about plotting iteration vs. f(x^t)-f^* for both Adam and AdaM^3.


10. In section 5.2, the authors claim that AdaM^3 is tuning-friendly. I would like to point out that Adam and AdamW also very tuning-friendly. alpha=0.001, beta_1=0.9, and beta_2=0.999 are the default setting, and I usually simply use these settings without changing them at all.


11. Regarding the results in Table 2, I wonder why the authors use very large models for CIFAR10 classification. VGGNet-16, ResNet34, and DenseNet-121 are designed for ImageNet classification. In contrast, ResNet20, ResNet56, etc., are designed for classifying CIFAR10. See Table 6 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.03385.pdf for details. I wonder why the test perplexity of LSTMs trained by Adam on Penn Treebank dataset in Table 4 is much worse than that reported in the paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.02182.pdf


12. Overall, I doubt the proposed algorithm can replace the role of SGD and Adam in today’s deep learning practice. We can certify this by seeing what will happen in five years.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is generally clear and sort of easy to follow.


Quality: The contribution of the paper is marginal and I am not convinced of the theoretical and practical contribution of this paper.


Reproducibility: Not available.
content.summary_of_the_review: As there are many weaknesses in this paper, I would argue for rejecting this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes another variant of Adam to improve the generalization performance of Adam. The authors proposes to change the gradient in the denominator of Adam by the momentum term. The authors then show some intuitions of why the proposed algorithm is better than Adam, and provide the convergence analysis of the AdaM. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm generalizes better than Adam and SGD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
  1. The proposed algorithm is very easy to implement
  2. The authors provide some intuitions of why the algorithm works better than Adam
  3. The experimental results validate most of the claims made by the authors

Weaknesses:
  1. I believe this modification of Adam still suffers from the same convergence problem as mentioned by Reddi et al. 2018 [1] because if we set $\beta_1 = 0$, the algorithm basically becomes RMSProp because momentum becomes just gradient. As discussed in [1], RMSProp has convergence issues in even simple online convex problems. Therefore, this algorithm has the same problem. This can also be observed in Theorem 4 in the Appendix B of this paper, where the authors have simply assumed that $v_t < v_{t+1}$. However, this assumption is basically saying the denominator keeps becoming larger and larger, which is very strong since in the online case, we can never know what the future gradients will be.

  2. Although the authors provide some intuitions of why the proposed algorithm behaves better than Adam, there is no theoretical benefit in general nonconvex/convex problems, which basically means the algorithm converges with the same speed as Adam (asymptotically). As can be observed from the images in the Appendix, the proposed algorithm is actually slower than the baselines in many experiments. There is also no theoretical benefit in terms of the generalization benefit.

  3. The proposed modification is two-fold, one is from the change of gradient into momentum, and the other one is the change of the $\epsilon$. I would like to see an ablation study of the two factors because there is a recent study that says, basically changing the $\epsilon$ to be larger in Adam can give better performance. [2] Since in this work the authors also propose to (almost equivalently) have a larger $\epsilon$, I wonder whether the change in performance simply comes from the bigger $\epsilon$.



[1]. Sashank J Reddi, Satyen Kale, and Sanjiv Kumar. On the convergence of adam and beyond. ICLR, 2018b.

[2] Wei Yuan, Kai-Xin Gao EAdam Optimizer: How $\epsilon$ Impact Adam. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.02150
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly clear, some-what novel, and reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: I agree that the paper has a lot of experimental results to prove the benefits of the proposed algorithm, and the results are fairly easy to follow. However, I am unsatisfied with its current form because of the non convergence issue, the lack of theoretical motivations, and whether the benefit in performance comes from $\epsilon$.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new adaptive optimizer, AdaM3, where an EMA of the squared momentum is used in the denominator and where epsilon is used differently. Experiments compare against SGD and other adaptive methods on task such as image classification on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, language modelling and NMT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper clearly describes AdaM3 and how it differs from Adam, and provides some intuition on how each of the two modifications work.
- There are experiments on multiple tasks and including different network architectures.

Weaknessess:
- The paper claims that Theorem 1 significantly improves the converge analysis of adaptive methods by not requiring that $\beta_{1,t}$ and $\frac{\alpha_t}{\sqrt {v_t}}$ to be monotonically decreasing. The proof techniques from prior work, however, often do not require these assumptions at all, and these are typically assumed to have a cleaner statement (e.g. O(log T / T) convergence instead of explicit dependencies on $\beta_{1,t}$ and so on). See the proof of Lemma 6.4 and 6.5 in [1]: the terms $T_3$ and $T_4$ can be written in terms of sums involving $\beta_{1,t}$ directly without assuming monotonicity, hence the upper bound in Theorem 3.1 can also be written as such. Note that this doesn't result in a convergence guarantee for any choice of $\beta_{1,t}$, but Theorem 1 in the submission also doesn't offer a guarantee if, say, $\beta_{1,t} = 0.9$. Also see Appendix E in [2] for a bound as function of $\alpha_t$ and its proof to see how the bound can be written with $\beta_{1,t}$ explicitly.
- It is unclear whether the main ingredient of AdaM3 is the EMA of the squared momentum or the different location of epsilon. The way that epsilon is used in AdaM3 (and in AdaBelief) has very significant implications on how the optimizer behaves (see Theorem 2 and experiments of [2], which show that large fixed epsilon or increasing epsilon lead to more SGD-like behavior and final performance). On the more meaningful tasks, there is either no comparison against AdaBelief (ImageNet) or the results are marginally better (NMT).
- The paper states one of its goals to design an adaptive method that generalizes as well as SGD, and while on ImageNet it achieves similar performance, previous adaptive methods are capable of outperforming SGD on ImageNet by bigger margins (see [2]).


[1] On the Convergence of A Class of Adam-Type Algorithms for Non-Convex Optimization - https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02941.pdf

[2] Domain-Independent Dominance of Adaptive Methods - https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/supplemental/Savarese_Domain-Independent_Dominance_of_CVPR_2021_supplemental.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: It is hard to evaluate the novelty since there are no ablative experiments showing the effect of the two modifications separately. One of the modifications (relocation of epsilon) has already been adopted and studied.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea is interesting and simple, but the novelty is limited and the results on more relevant tasks aren't as promising.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
